title: Stop Ordering AI Takeout  A Cookbook for Winning When You Build In House - Jan Siml

primary.label: AI Product, UX & Human Factors
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The talk centers on product design choices, UX strategy, and human-in-the-loop feedback for an in-house GenAI application rather than model internals or infrastructure. The system is an internal enterprise sales assistant embedded in B2B workflows with measurable revenue impact. Covers the build-versus-buy decision through production deployment and ongoing optimization via user feedback loops. Assumes working knowledge of GenAI development and enterprise product strategy but is broadly accessible to practitioners. A 10-minute lightning talk delivered at the AI Engineer conference. All claims are the speaker's first-person account with no external validation or peer review.

summary: Jan Siml contends that many AI teams run their strategy like ordering takeout—picking flashy solutions that look good online but underperform in practice. He advocates a home-cooked approach where small teams focus on one painful job-to-be-done with a clear dollar-based outcome. In Q1 2024, his team of two developers spent roughly 10 sprint weeks building an internal GenAI sales assistant that generated several million dollars in ARR and won a group-level award. He contrasts the Twitter recipe—giant eval suites, multi-agent systems, cutting-edge models—with a pragmatic in-house approach. SaaS is like a hotel buffet: generic but safe. In-house shines when you own the data, know the workflows, and sit next to your users. The rule of thumb: buy SaaS to explore the unknown; build in-house once the workflow is yours. He then presents five lessons that work best as a set. First, go absurdly deep on one painful job-to-be-done with an identifiable value event. Second, trace every click to dollars—offline evals are smoke alarms, not contracts; instrument everything to link AI tasks to revenue. Third, push proactively via daily digests and zero-click nudges rather than waiting for users to visit a chat UI; this produced 20 NPS points higher and an order of magnitude higher engagement. Fourth, convert time-saved into time-well-spent by guiding users to high-value activities instead of letting freed time fill with low-value work. Fifth, invest in data, integrations, and UX over bigger models—larger models were 60x more expensive and 10x slower than 4o-mini with no visible quality difference. Siml describes a revenue flywheel: tight feedback loops make users feel heard, generating improvement ideas, enabling better experiments, driving adoption, and producing more prioritization data. He closes by advising teams to start small, follow the money, and let users guide development.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: The AI Takeout Problem
sections.summary: Siml opens by comparing hype-driven AI strategies to ordering disappointing takeout—expectations set by LinkedIn/Twitter are too high for internal needs, like paying for truffles on instant noodles. His team followed a different recipe that delivered millions in revenue.

sections.title: Build Proof and ARR Results
sections.summary: In Q1 2024 the team chose build over buy with two developers and roughly 10 sprint weeks, producing several million dollars in ARR and a group-level award—enough for finance to stop questioning the build decision.

sections.title: When to Build vs. Buy
sections.summary: Siml critiques the Twitter recipe (giant evals, multi-agent, cutting-edge models) as overkill for in-house needs. SaaS is a hotel buffet—generic but safe. In-house wins when you own the data, know the workflows, sit next to users, and reuse existing infra. Rule of thumb: buy to explore, build in-house once the workflow is yours.

sections.title: Lesson 1: Go Deep on One Job-to-Be-Done
sections.summary: In-house lets you go absurdly deep on one painful job-to-be-done with a pinpointable dollar-based value event. The team started with a simple sales alert use case and grew from there by talking to users. Staying focused keeps things simple and avoids agentic complexity.

sections.title: Lesson 2: Trace Every Click to Dollars
sections.summary: Offline evals are smoke alarms, not contracts—nobody at the board meeting asks for F1 or NDCG. Instrument everything from start to the value event so you can say this AI task led to $20. Linking system to dollars shifts conversations to idea ROI. Automate performance reports and build leaderboards to surface champions and help struggling users.

sections.title: Lesson 3: Push, Don't Wait
sections.summary: Don't wait for users to come to you. The best UI is the one you never need to use. The team built daily digest notifications pushing what users need to know today. Chat UI remained as a fallback for unexpected tasks. Proactive delivery produced 20 NPS points higher and an order of magnitude higher engagement than the chat app.

sections.title: Lesson 4: Convert Time-Saved into Time-Well-Spent
sections.summary: AI must guide action, not just deliver information. Saving 30 minutes is worthless if users fill it with email sludge. Convert freed time into high-value activities by understanding the revenue funnel and diverting user attention accordingly.

sections.title: Lesson 5: Data and UX vs. Bigger Models
sections.summary: Good data consistently beats great models. Larger models (o3-class) are 60x more expensive and 10x slower than 4o-mini, with the only production-visible difference being cost. The best results came from adding more triggers and going deeper on user needs—boring but effective. Build for what users need, not what you want to try.

sections.title: The Revenue Flywheel and Recap
sections.summary: Tight feedback loops make users feel heard, sparking improvement ideas that drive experiments, adoption, and more data—spinning a revenue flywheel. Recap: focus on one painful job-to-be-done, track dollars not eval metrics, push proactively, channel time savings to high-value work, and invest in basics. Start small, follow the money, let users guide you.
